To tackle unserved retail needs, the company approved a capacity expansion of 2.25 lakh units annually. Launch Rapid Reads → AI-POWERED 
 Electric two-wheeler maker Ather Energy reported its first profit in the September quarter, becoming the first major standalone EV company in India to turn a profit.
 Net income for the quarter was Rs 1.26 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 154 crore a year earlier. Its shares closed the day 14 percent higher on the NSE. The results were announced during market hours.
 Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Tarun Mehta, however, said the company isn't watching profit most closely.
 “PAT [profit after tax] is not the first thing to focus on,” Mehta said on an earnings call. The priority is the top line and volume, which bring operating leverage, he said.
 To enhance capacity, the board approved an expansion plan on Monday. Ather will add 2.25 lakh units of annual capacity, taking the total to about 11.4 lakh by the September quarter of fiscal 2028, compared with the 9.2 lakh units previously planned. It will invest about Rs 122 crore across its two sites: Hosur in Tamil Nadu and its new facility in Auric City in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar.

 “If all the capacity work that we are putting in bears fruit well over the next few months, then I believe that PAT will take care of itself,” Mehta said, adding that profit “can go up and down” in the near term.
 Ather’s startup rival Ola Electric remains loss-making. Bigger rivals are better placed. Bajaj Auto’s EV business, spanning two- and three-wheelers, already runs at double-digit Ebitda margins. TVS Motor doesn’t report its EV profitability separately.
 EV sales have surged since the Iran war broke out in March and have continued. Ather said pre-orders more than doubled to 1.80 lakh in the quarter, while enquiries also rose 109 percent to about 10 lakh.
 Its Hosur plant ran at 98 percent utilisation at peak production, and Ather made about 33,000 vehicles a month on average, up from 28,000 in the June quarter. Mehta said the company is leaving roughly 20,000 units a month of retail demand unserved.

 With the approved expansion plan, Hosur capacity will rise by 75,000 units a year, from 4.2 lakh to 4.95 lakh, by December.
 The Auric plant will begin phased commercial production in December, with Phase 1 at 5 lakh units a year, or about 42,000 a month. Another 12,000 units a month, taking annual capacity to 6.5 lakh, is due by the September quarter of FY28.

 Mehta said trial production at Auric should begin in the coming weeks and installation will be complete by the March quarter.
 The base capacity will take about two quarters to ramp up fully.
 Even with both plants, he said, monthly capacity of 77,000 units would leave little headroom against current demand of 50,000-60,000 a month, which is why the expansion was brought forward.
 In the quarter gone by, Ather’s revenue rose 62 percent to Rs 1,527 crore, while wholesale volume rose 42 percent to 93,211 units. Revenue per vehicle was about Rs 1.57 lakh.
 It reported Ebitda of Rs 74.2 crore, a margin of 4.9 percent against a negative 9.6 percent a year earlier, an improvement of about 1,450 basis points. It was the second straight positive quarter, after a margin of 0.8 percent in the June quarter.
 The average ex-showroom price rose to about Rs 1,64,000 from about Rs 1,50,000 in the March quarter. Ather attributed that to price increases and a richer product mix.
Its non-vehicle revenue rose to 15 percent of revenue from operations from 12 percent a year earlier. Some 94 percent of buyers took the AtherStack Pro software pack. More than half of non-vehicle revenue comes from that pack, which Mehta said carries gross margins of 80-90 percent.

 Commodity pressure
 Adjusted gross margin was 24 percent, up 160 basis points from a year earlier, though below the 25.4 percent of the March quarter.
 Aluminium, copper, lithium and plastics stayed expensive through the quarter. Mehta said hopes of relief earlier this year, tied to a resolution of the Hormuz crisis, proved wrong. He said aluminium has shown some signs of cooling in recent days.
 “We are not out of the woods,” Mehta said. He called the commodity squeeze temporary but said it has lasted “a few quarters longer” than he expected.
 Ather doesn’t plan more price increases in the December quarter, he said, and commodity costs look broadly flat for now.
 Industry registrations rose 82 percent to about 5.98 lakh units, and electric penetration of scooter sales reached 11.2 percent for the quarter, up from 7.8 percent. It hit a record 11.6 percent in September.
 Ather’s own registrations, including exports, rose about 60 percent to 92,500 units, trailing the industry. Its market share slipped to 15.1 percent from 17.2 percent a year earlier.
 The Bengaluru-based company launched its new mass-market e-scooter, the Konarc, on August 29. Built on a new platform, the company says the scooter is aimed at petrol buyers.
 Fewer than 10,000 Konarcs were sold in September, and only in a few northern markets.
 Mehta said enquiries, pre-orders and walk-ins there were “up several times”. He said the early reaction was that it is “finally a proper scooter, and not just an electric one.”
